# The all-dimensional stochastic capacity dual and the zero-row boundary

This note establishes an exact support criterion and a general boundary
case of the higher-dimensional stochastic question. It does not prove the
question for matrices having positive rows when d>=3. It also records an
exact obstruction to replacing uniform simplex measure by an arbitrary
probability distribution on the probability simplex.

## 1. Definitions

Fix d>=1 and m=d+1. Let Xi be uniform on the barycentric d-simplex. For a
nonnegative row x of length m, let

    F_x(t)=Pr(x dot Xi<=t),
    phi_d(x)=inf_{t>0, F_x(t)>0} t/F_x(t)^(1/d).

Write GM_d for the geometric mean of d nonnegative numbers. Let D_d be

    {v in R_+^m: there is Y>=0 with Y_ii=0, sum_i Y_ij=1,
                   v_i<=GM_d((Y_ij)_{j!=i}) for every i}.

The set of allowed Y is compact and convex. Geometric mean is concave and
coordinatewise nondecreasing, so D_d is a compact convex downward set.
One self-contained concavity proof is the AM-GM representation

    GM_d(z)=inf{(sum_j a_j z_j)/d: a_j>0, product_j a_j=1}.

For positive z equality is attained at a_j=GM(z)/z_j; zero-entry cases
follow by choosing the corresponding coefficients to tend to infinity
and balancing the remaining coefficients. The infimum of linear functions
is concave. Concavity and homogeneity also give superadditivity
GM(u+v)>=GM(u)+GM(v).

## 2. Exact support dual, including zero weights

For c>=0, the support function of D_d is

    h_D(c)=min {sum_j lambda_j: lambda>=0,
                 c_i<=d (product_{j!=i}lambda_j)^(1/d) for all i}.   (1)

Weak duality is rowwise AM-GM. For every feasible lambda and Y,

    c_i GM(Y_i,off)<=d GM((lambda_j Y_ij)_{j!=i})
                      <=sum_{j!=i}lambda_j Y_ij.

Summation gives the required upper bound.

Here is a finite-dimensional proof of the reverse inequality without any
boundary differentiability assumption. For epsilon>0 maximize the smooth
concave function

    H_epsilon(Y)=sum_i c_i GM((Y_ij+epsilon)_{j!=i})

over the compact allowed Y. At a maximizer, for each column j let
lambda_j be the largest partial derivative among its off-diagonal entries.
A transfer within that column shows that every positive entry has this
largest derivative. Hence

    sum_j lambda_j=sum_{i!=j}Y_ij partial_ij H_epsilon
                  <=H_epsilon(Y).

Each partial derivative in row i is

    c_i GM(Y_i,off+epsilon)/[d(Y_ij+epsilon)].

Their product over j!=i is exactly (c_i/d)^d. Since every lambda_j is at
least the corresponding derivative, lambda is feasible in (1), also when
c_i=0. The regularized objectives converge uniformly to H_0 on the compact
matrix domain by uniform continuity of geometric mean. Therefore the dual
infimum is at most h_D(c), proving equality. The dual feasible set is
closed and nonempty; bounded sum sublevels are compact. Its infimum is
thus a minimum. This handles zero lambda and zero c without a limiting
claim about selected matrices.

## 3. Homogeneous polynomial criterion

For v>=0, membership in D_d is equivalent to

    sum_i p_i^d - d sum_i v_i product_{j!=i}p_j >=0
                    for every p in R_+^m.                         (2)

Necessity follows from (1) by taking lambda_j=p_j^d and
c_i=d product_{j!=i}p_j. For sufficiency take arbitrary c>=0 and a minimizing
lambda in (1). Put p_j=lambda_j^(1/d). Then c_i<=d product_{j!=i}p_j,
so (2) gives c dot v<=sum lambda=h_D(c).

These nonnegative supporting inequalities characterize a compact convex
downward set. Explicitly, if v>=0 lies outside D_d and w is its nearest
point in D_d, then c=v-w separates v strictly from D_d. The projection
inequality gives c dot(z-w)<=0 for every z in D_d. If w_i>0, testing a
small decrease in coordinate i gives c_i>=0; if w_i=0, c_i=v_i>=0.
Thus c>=0, contradicting the supporting inequalities.

When d=2, (2) is exactly positivity on the nonnegative orthant of the
three-cycle quadratic; its negative off-diagonal signs make this
positive semidefiniteness on all of R^3. It reduces to
sum v_i^2+2product v_i<=1. When d=1, D_1=[0,1]^2, as also follows
immediately from (2).

One useful exact support example is the following. If lambda_j>0,
sum lambda=dT, and every lambda_i<=T, set

    c_i=d(product_{j!=i}lambda_j)^(1/d),
    Y_ij=(T-lambda_i)/lambda_j for i!=j,  Y_ii=0.

Its column sums are one. Direct multiplication shows
c_i GM(Y_i,off)=d(T-lambda_i), including a zero row when lambda_i=T.
The sum is dT=sum lambda, so this Y attains the support bound (1).

## 4. Exact rows with zeros

If x has exactly one zero, then

    phi_d(x)=GM_d(the other d entries).                           (3)

Choose the zero-entry barycentric vertex as the coordinate origin. The
uniform simplex becomes {u>=0: sum u<=1}, and x dot Xi is the positive
linear form x' dot u. Scaling u=t v shows that F_x(t)/t^d is nonincreasing
in t. For 0<t<=min x'_j, the constraint sum u<=1 is redundant on
{x' dot u<=t}, and the normalized cap volume is exactly

    F_x(t)=t^d/product_j x'_j.

This proves (3) globally, not only near zero.

If x has at least two zeros, then phi_d(x)=0. For d>=2, in the same
coordinates one zero-cost coordinate can range over a fixed interval
while the remaining positive-cost coordinates have ranges proportional
to t; a small such box remains inside sum u<=1. Its volume is at least
C t^(d-1), for a fixed C>0 and sufficiently small t, so
 t/F_x(t)^(1/d) tends to zero. Additional zero-cost coordinates only
increase this lower bound. An all-zero row has F_x(t)=1 for t>0, and in
d=1 the only multiple-zero case is precisely this all-zero row.

## 5. Every row having a zero is sufficient in every dimension

**Theorem.** If X is a nonnegative column-stochastic m by m matrix and
every row has at least one zero entry, then

    (phi_d(X_1),...,phi_d(X_m)) belongs to D_d.                     (4)

Fix arbitrary weights c_i>=0. Rows with multiple zeros contribute zero
by Section 4 and can initially be left aside. Group the remaining rows
according to their unique zero column. In each nonempty group choose a
row index i having largest c_i, replace that row by the sum of all rows
in the group, and set the other rows of the group to zero. Geometric-mean
superadditivity gives

    sum_{r in group} c_r phi_d(X_r)
       <=c_i sum_{r in group} GM(X_r,off)
       <=c_i GM(sum_{r in group}X_r,off).

The surviving rows have different zero columns. Permute columns to put
the zero of each surviving row on its own diagonal; this is possible
because the partial matching is injective. Ignore all remaining rows,
leaving their column masses unallocated. In every column allocate this
remaining nonnegative mass to any off-diagonal row. Such a row exists
because m>=2. Existing surviving-row entries can only increase.

The resulting matrix Y is zero-diagonal and column-stochastic. Its
weighted geometric-mean objective is at least c dot phi_d(X). Hence
c dot phi_d(X)<=h_D(c) for every c>=0. The characterization in Section 3
proves (4). The constructed Y may depend on c; this is legitimate because
compact convex downward separation is used, not a claim of one universal
coordinatewise dominating construction from the merging procedure.

## 6. Why an arbitrary-probability replacement is false already for d=2

An independently certified archived coupling has Beta(2,1) marginals
V_1,V_2,V_3 on [0,1] and

    2V_1+V_2+V_3<=273/100 almost surely.

Its exact finite rational certificate and verifier are
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/beta_coupling_exact_certificate_root.json` and
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/certify_beta_coupling_exact_root.py`. The construction lifts a finite-bin
coupling using conditional Beta distributions, so this is an exact
continuous-marginal assertion, not a grid extrapolation.

Put a=(200,100,100)/273 and W_i=a_i V_i. Their sum is at most one.
Set Z_1=W_1+1-sum W_i and Z_2=W_2,Z_3=W_3. This is a random point of the
probability simplex and Z_i>=W_i for each i. Consequently, for t>0,

    Pr(Z_i<=t)<=Pr(a_i V_i<=t)<= (t/a_i)^2,

where the right side is harmless when it exceeds one. Thus the capacity
inf_t t/sqrt(Pr(Z_i<=t)) is at least a_i. Nevertheless a is outside D_2:

    sum a_i^2+2product a_i-1 = 33583/20346417 >0.

There is also a rational support witness for (2). For
p=(200/273,1,1),

    sum p_i^2-2sum_i a_i product_{j!=i}p_j=-142/74529<0.

Thus the probability-simplex constraint, the marginal capacity bounds,
and even these exact continuous marginal laws do not imply membership
in D_d. The unproved full higher-dimensional stochastic question must
retain its actual uniform-simplex affine-image structure.
